label: Oscillations
notes: Chapter five takes a Lagrangian system near a stable equilibrium and shows that, to leading order, every such system is a bundle of independent harmonic oscillators. We motivate why linearization is the right first move and preview the three pillars: quadratic energy forms, simultaneous diagonalization, and normal modes oscillating at characteristic frequencies.

label: Equilibrium and Linearization
notes: An equilibrium is a critical point of the potential; stability means it is a strict local minimum. We expand the potential to second order, drop the constant and the vanishing linear term, and keep the Hessian. The kinetic energy is already quadratic in velocities, evaluated at the equilibrium configuration. That pairing of two quadratic forms is the whole subject.

label: Two Quadratic Forms
notes: After linearization the Lagrangian is one half q-dot transpose A q-dot minus one half q transpose B q. Matrix A, the mass or metric matrix, is symmetric positive definite. Matrix B, the stiffness matrix, is the potential Hessian and is positive definite exactly when the equilibrium is stable. Everything else is linear algebra applied to this pair.

label: Linearized Equations
notes: The Euler-Lagrange equations become A q double-dot plus B q equals zero, a linear system with constant coefficients. We seek solutions of the form a vector times a sine of omega t. Substituting turns the differential equation into an algebraic eigenvalue condition, replacing calculus with a determinant. This is the bridge from dynamics to spectral linear algebra.

label: Generalized Eigenvalue Problem
notes: The ansatz produces B v equals omega squared A v, a generalized eigenvalue problem with metric A. Because A is positive definite and B symmetric, all eigenvalues omega squared are real, and stability forces them positive, giving real frequencies. The characteristic polynomial det of B minus omega squared A equals zero supplies the spectrum of frequencies.

label: Simultaneous Diagonalization
notes: The central theorem: two quadratic forms, one positive definite, can be simultaneously reduced. A linear change of coordinates makes A the identity and B diagonal at once. Geometrically we first sphere the metric, then rotate to the principal axes of the potential. The eigenvectors are A-orthogonal, which is exactly the orthogonality the modes inherit.

label: Normal Coordinates and Modes
notes: In the new coordinates the Lagrangian splits into a sum of uncoupled one-dimensional oscillators. Each normal coordinate Q i obeys Q i double-dot plus omega i squared Q i equals zero and rings at its own frequency. A normal mode is the motion in which only one normal coordinate is excited, so the whole system moves rigidly in a single shape at a single frequency.

label: Coupled Oscillators: Two Modes
notes: The two-mass spring chain is the canonical example. Its symmetric mode moves both masses together, leaving the coupling spring relaxed, so it oscillates at the bare frequency. Its antisymmetric mode moves the masses oppositely, stretching the coupling maximally, so it sits higher. Drawing both shapes makes the abstract eigenvectors physically concrete and memorable.

label: Characteristic Spectrum
notes: Collecting the roots of the characteristic equation gives the frequency spectrum, one line per mode. The two-mass example shows a low symmetric line and a higher antisymmetric line, with the gap set by the coupling strength. Reading a spectrum like this is how one diagnoses a vibrating structure without integrating any trajectory.

label: Superposition of Modes
notes: Because the linearized system is linear, the general motion is an arbitrary superposition of normal modes, each with its own amplitude and phase fixed by initial conditions. Generic motion is therefore quasi-periodic, not periodic, unless the frequencies are commensurable. The normal modes form the natural basis in which initial data decompose cleanly.

label: Perturbation and Parametric Resonance
notes: When a parameter of the system is driven periodically, the equilibrium can lose stability even with no direct forcing. The pendulum with vibrating support obeys a Hill or Mathieu equation. Stability tongues in the parameter plane mark where small oscillations blow up, most violently when the drive frequency is near twice a natural frequency. A vibrating support can even stabilize the inverted pendulum.

label: Summary
notes: We reduced any stable Lagrangian equilibrium to independent harmonic oscillators through three moves: linearize into two quadratic forms, solve the generalized eigenvalue problem, and read off normal modes and frequencies. Superposition handles general motion, and parametric driving opens the door to resonance and stability tongues. This linear core underlies perturbation theory throughout mechanics.
